blocks.m: Fuel delivery – can cause hesitation, stalling or no-start.
Generic powertrain code (fuel/air metering & auxiliary emission controls).
The engine computer can't electrically control a variable cam timing (VVT) oil control solenoid.
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the solenoid
Low or very dirty engine oil
k: Inspect the solenoid connector and wiring for damage or oil in the connector
Measure solenoid resistance against the service spec
Check the oil level and condition

blocks.m: Actual cam timing doesn't match what the computer commanded.
c: Low oil level, wrong oil viscosity, or an overdue oil change
Sticking oil control solenoid or clogged solenoid screen
Stretched timing chain or worn cam phaser (higher mileage engines)
k: Check oil level; change oil with the grade specified on the oil cap/manual
Clear the code and see whether it returns after the oil change
If it returns with a rattle at start-up, have the timing chain inspected

blocks.m: Engine timing/position sensing – can cause stalling or no-start.
Crankshaft and camshaft positions don't line up the way they should.
c: Faulty cam or crank position sensor
k: Note any other cam/crank/VVT codes stored with it
Listen for timing chain rattle on cold start
If the engine runs rough or rattles loudly, stop driving: a jumped chain can wreck the engine

blocks.m: The heater inside an oxygen sensor isn't working, so the sensor is slow to start reading after a cold start.
c: Failed O2 sensor heater element (replace the sensor)
Blown fuse for the O2 heater circuit
k: Check the O2 heater fuse
Measure heater resistance at the sensor connector (typically a few ohms)
Inspect the harness for melted or chafed wires near the exhaust

blocks.m: An oxygen sensor heater circuit fault – mainly affects emissions after cold starts.
Boost control – expect reduced power.
An oxygen/air-fuel sensor issue – can affect fuel control and economy.
A downstream oxygen sensor issue – mainly emissions monitoring.
Airflow readings (MAF/MAP) don't agree with the throttle position.
c: Vacuum or intake air leak after the throttle
k: Inspect intake boots and vacuum hoses for cracks
Clean the throttle body and MAF sensor

blocks.m: Fuel pressure is lower than the computer wants. The engine may hesitate, run lean or stall.
c: Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
k: Refuel and see if it recurs
Compare fuel rail pressure at idle and under load
Have fuel pressure checked with a mechanical gauge

blocks.m: Fuel pressure is higher than the computer wants.
c: Stuck fuel pressure regulator or pressure control valve
k: Compare fuel rail pressure to spec
Check the pressure sensor wiring

blocks.m: The mass air flow (MAF) sensor reading is missing or doesn't make sense. The engine may hesitate, stall or run poorly.
c: Dirty MAF sensor (oil from oiled air filters is a classic cause)
Air leak between the MAF and the throttle body (cracked intake boot)
Unplugged, corroded or damaged MAF connector
k: Inspect the intake boot between the MAF and throttle for cracks or loose clamps
Clean the MAF with dedicated MAF cleaner (never touch the element)
Check that the air filter isn't clogged
At warm idle, MAF is roughly 2–7 g/s for most 4-cylinder engines and rises smoothly with RPM

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (fuel and air metering).
The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor reading is out of range.
c: Cracked or disconnected MAP vacuum hose
k: With the key on and engine off, MAP should read close to barometric pressure
At warm idle it should drop well below barometric (roughly 25–45 kPa)

blocks.m: The intake air temperature (IAT) sensor reading is missing or out of range.
c: Unplugged or corroded connector (the IAT is often built into the MAF)
Wiring fault (P0113 is usually an open circuit)
k: After the car has sat overnight, IAT should be close to the ambient temperature

blocks.m: The engine coolant temperature sensor reading is missing or implausible. The temperature gauge and cooling fans may not be reliable.
c: For P0116: thermostat stuck open, or low coolant
k: Watch coolant temperature: it should climb steadily to about 85–105 °C
Check the coolant level with the engine cold
Keep an eye on the gauge; don't rely on the fans running automatically until it's fixed

blocks.m: Cooling system – watch engine temperature.
A throttle position sensor signal is faulty or the two throttle sensors disagree. The car often drops into reduced-power (limp) mode.
c: Dirty or failing electronic throttle body
k: Inspect the throttle body connector
Clean the throttle body, then do the manufacturer's idle/throttle relearn
Throttle position should move smoothly with no jumps as the pedal is pressed

blocks.m: Throttle/pedal control – may cause reduced-power (limp) mode.
The engine takes too long to warm up, or never reaches normal temperature.
c: Thermostat stuck open (by far the most common)
k: Coolant should reach roughly 85–105 °C within 10–15 minutes of driving
Weak cabin heat and worse fuel economy are typical symptoms

blocks.m: An upstream oxygen sensor (before the catalytic converter) is faulty or its signal is abnormal. This sensor is used for fuel control.
c: A real lean (low voltage) or rich (high voltage) condition rather than a bad sensor
k: Look for exhaust leaks at the manifold
Check fuel trims: large trims point to a real fuelling problem, not the sensor
A healthy narrow-band upstream sensor switches rapidly between about 0.1 and 0.9 V at warm idle
Fix before long trips: running rich hurts economy and the catalytic converter

blocks.m: A downstream oxygen sensor (after the catalytic converter) is faulty. It mainly monitors the converter and has little effect on how the engine runs.
k: A downstream sensor should read fairly steady (often 0.5–0.8 V) once the converter is warm

blocks.m: The engine is running lean: too much air or not enough fuel, and the computer has run out of room to correct it.
c: Vacuum leak (cracked hose, PCV valve/hose, intake manifold gasket)
Weak fuel pump, clogged fuel filter, or low fuel pressure
Exhaust leak before the upstream O2 sensor
k: Add short- and long-term trims together: above about +10% means the computer is adding fuel
High at idle but better at 2,500 rpm points to a vacuum leak
High at all speeds points to fuel delivery or the MAF
Listen for hissing around the intake; a smoke test finds leaks quickly

blocks.m: The engine is running rich: too much fuel, and the computer can't pull enough out.
k: Trims well below about -10% mean the computer is removing fuel
Check the air filter
Check coolant temperature reads correctly when warm

blocks.m: The fuel rail pressure sensor signal is out of range.
k: Compare rail pressure with the engine off, at idle, and under load

blocks.m: The computer sees an electrical fault in one fuel injector circuit. That cylinder will likely misfire.
c: Injector driver fault in the engine computer (rare)
k: Measure injector resistance and compare with the other injectors
Inspect the injector connector for corrosion or a broken lock tab

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (fuel and air metering (injector circuit)).
The engine is overheating.
k: Pull over and turn the engine off; driving an overheating engine can warp the head
Never open a hot radiator cap
Once cool, check the coolant level and look for leaks
Check that the cooling fans run when the engine is hot

blocks.m: Something (coolant, oil or transmission fluid) is too hot – pull over and let it cool.
Engine speed went above the safe limit.
c: Over-revving (a missed shift or aggressive downshift)
k: A one-off event can be cleared; if it keeps returning without over-revving, have the crank sensor checked

blocks.m: Fault in the fuel pump control circuit. The car may stall or fail to start.
k: Check the fuel pump fuse and relay
Listen for the pump priming when the key turns on

blocks.m: Turbo boost pressure went higher than allowed. The engine usually cuts power to protect itself.
c: Disconnected or split wastegate vacuum line
k: Inspect the wastegate actuator and its hoses
Avoid full throttle until it's fixed

blocks.m: The turbo isn't making as much boost as requested. Expect low power.
c: Boost leak (split intercooler hose, loose clamp)
k: Inspect intercooler pipes and couplers for oil residue or splits
Listen for whistling or hissing under boost

blocks.m: Random or multiple cylinders are misfiring. If the check-engine light is FLASHING, stop: severe misfires overheat and destroy the catalytic converter.
k: Check when the plugs were last replaced
Check fuel trims for a lean condition
Note whether it happens at idle, under load, or when cold

blocks.m: One cylinder is misfiring. If the check-engine light is FLASHING, stop: severe misfires overheat and destroy the catalytic converter.
c: Low compression (valve, ring or head gasket)
k: Swap that cylinder's coil with a neighbour's, clear codes, drive: if the misfire moves, replace the coil
Pull and inspect the spark plug
If the misfire stays put after swapping coil and plug, have a compression test done

blocks.m: A misfire was detected. If the check-engine light is flashing, stop driving.
Generic powertrain code (ignition system or misfire).
The engine speed/crankshaft position signal is missing or erratic. The engine can stall or fail to start without warning.
c: Metal debris on the sensor tip
k: Watch RPM for dropouts or jumps while the engine runs
Symptoms often get worse when the engine is hot

blocks.m: Knock sensing – the engine may reduce timing, lowering power.
Knock sensor circuit fault. The computer retards ignition timing as a precaution, so power and economy drop.
c: Damaged wiring (often under the intake manifold)
k: Inspect the knock sensor harness
Avoid heavy loads and use the recommended fuel octane until fixed

blocks.m: The camshaft position sensor signal is missing or incorrect. Starting may take longer, and the engine can stall.
k: Inspect the sensor connector for oil intrusion
If other timing codes are present, check the timing chain

blocks.m: Ignition – likely to cause misfires.
Electrical fault in one ignition coil circuit (coil A = cylinder 1, B = 2, and so on). That cylinder will misfire.
c: Coil driver fault in the engine computer (rare)
k: Swap the coil with another cylinder and see if the code follows it
Inspect the connector

blocks.m: Body/convenience feature.
Too little exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) flow was detected.
c: Carbon-clogged EGR passages or valve (most common)
Vacuum or solenoid fault on vacuum-operated valves
On older Fords: the DPFE pressure sensor or its hoses
k: Clean the EGR valve and passages
Inspect EGR vacuum lines and the pressure sensor hoses

blocks.m: EGR flow is excessive, or the EGR control circuit is faulty. Excess EGR can cause rough idle or stalling.
k: Rough idle that improves when the EGR is unplugged points to a stuck-open valve

blocks.m: Exhaust gas recirculation system – mainly emissions.
The secondary air injection system (which pumps air into the exhaust on cold starts) isn't working correctly.
k: Listen for the air pump running for about a minute after a cold start

blocks.m: Secondary air injection – mainly emissions on cold starts.
The catalytic converter isn't cleaning the exhaust as well as it should. The car drives normally but will likely fail an emissions inspection.
c: An engine problem that damaged the converter (misfire, burning oil, running rich)
k: Fix any misfire, lean or rich codes first: they cause and mask converter failure
Compare O2 sensors: the downstream one should be much steadier than the upstream one
In the US, catalytic converters carry a federal emissions warranty of 8 years / 80,000 miles

blocks.m: Catalytic converter system – mainly emissions.
The evaporative emissions (EVAP) system found a fuel vapour leak. No effect on driving.
c: Loose, missing or worn gas cap (check this first)
k: Tighten the gas cap until it clicks, or replace a cap with a cracked seal
Clear the code; the EVAP test only reruns after several days of normal driving
A smoke test finds small leaks

blocks.m: The EVAP purge valve isn't flowing correctly, or its circuit is faulty.
k: Hard starting right after refuelling is a common sign of a stuck-open purge valve

blocks.m: Evaporative emissions (fuel vapour) system – no effect on driving.
The EVAP vent valve or its circuit is faulty.
c: Vent valve clogged with dirt or debris
k: Trouble filling the tank (pump nozzle clicking off early) is a common sign
Inspect the vent valve near the charcoal canister

blocks.m: The fuel tank pressure sensor signal is out of range.
k: Inspect the sensor connector on or near the fuel tank

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (auxiliary emission controls).
The fuel level sensor signal is faulty. The fuel gauge may be wrong, so it's easy to run out.
c: Worn fuel level sender in the tank
k: Track fuel by trip distance until fixed
Compare the gauge with the fuel-level reading here

blocks.m: Fault in the cooling fan control circuit. The engine can overheat in traffic or at idle.
c: Fan control module or wiring fault
k: With the engine hot or the A/C on, the fan should run
Watch the coolant temperature in slow traffic

blocks.m: The vehicle speed signal is missing or implausible. Speedometer, shifting, cruise control and ABS may be affected.
c: Faulty vehicle speed sensor (or an ABS wheel speed sensor on many cars)
k: Compare the speed reading here with GPS speed
Check for ABS codes as well

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (vehicle speed, idle control and auxiliary inputs).
Brake-related – brake lights, ABS or cruise functions may be affected.
Idle speed isn't what the computer is targeting.
c: Dirty throttle body or idle air control valve
k: Clean the throttle body, then do the idle relearn procedure
Check for vacuum leaks

blocks.m: Charging/electrical supply – can leave you stranded.
The oil pressure sensor/switch signal is faulty. This could be a sensor fault or real low oil pressure.
c: Faulty oil pressure sensor or switch (a common leak point too)
Actual low oil pressure or level
k: Check the oil level right away
If the oil light is on or the engine is ticking or knocking, stop driving
Have oil pressure confirmed with a mechanical gauge

blocks.m: Oil pressure sensing fault – check the oil level now and watch the oil light.
Engine oil pressure is too low.
c: Worn oil pump or clogged pickup screen
k: Stop the engine as soon as it's safe: low oil pressure destroys bearings within minutes
Check the oil level
Don't drive it again until oil pressure is confirmed with a mechanical gauge

blocks.m: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor fault. The A/C may not work.
k: Inspect the sensor connector on the A/C line

blocks.m: Climate control – comfort only.
Steering system – assist or related features may be affected.
System voltage is too low. It can leave you stranded and cause odd faults in other modules.
k: Battery should read about 12.4–12.7 V with the engine off
About 13.5–14.7 V with the engine running (see the ⚡ voltage in the status bar)
Clean and tighten the battery terminals

blocks.m: System voltage is too high. Overcharging can damage the battery and electronics.
c: Bad voltage sense wire or ground
k: Voltage running should not exceed about 15 V

blocks.m: Brake switch circuit fault. Brake lights may not work, cruise control is usually disabled, and the shifter may not leave Park.
c: Faulty or misadjusted brake light switch
k: Have someone confirm the brake lights come on when the pedal is pressed

blocks.m: The engine computer has detected an internal or communication fault.
c: Low battery voltage or a bad ground (rule this out first)
Interrupted programming or software issue (P0602: often fixed by a dealer reflash)
k: Check battery voltage and the main ground straps
Ask a dealer about software updates for your VIN before replacing the module
P0603 alone after a battery disconnect often clears itself

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (computer and output circuits).
Fault in the alternator (generator) control circuit. The battery may not be charging.
c: Wiring or connector fault at the alternator
k: Running voltage should be about 13.5–14.7 V

blocks.m: The 5-volt sensor reference circuit is out of range. Several sensors can fail at once, often causing limp mode.
c: A shorted sensor on the shared 5 V reference circuit
k: Unplug sensors on that circuit one at a time; the code clearing points to the shorted one

blocks.m: Transmission – may cause harsh shifts, slipping or limp mode.
Fault in the check-engine light circuit. The light may not warn you of new problems.
c: Failed bulb/LED driver in the cluster
k: Check that the light comes on briefly at key-on
Scan for codes periodically until fixed

blocks.m: The transmission computer has stored a fault and asked for the check-engine light. The real code is in the transmission module.
c: Any transmission fault; see the codes listed from the transmission module (often 7E9)
k: Look for codes from the TCM in this list; they explain the actual problem
Check the transmission fluid level and condition

blocks.m: Transmission range (PRNDL) sensor fault. The car may not start in Park, show the wrong gear, or shift harshly.
k: Check that the dash gear display matches the lever in every position

blocks.m: Transmission fluid temperature sensor fault. Shifts may be harsh and torque converter lockup may be disabled.
c: Faulty fluid temperature sensor (often on the internal harness)
k: Check fluid level and condition

blocks.m: A transmission speed sensor signal is missing. Expect erratic shifting or limp mode (stuck in one gear).
c: Metal debris on the magnetic sensor tip
k: Check fluid level
Inspect the sensor and connector

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (transmission).
The transmission's measured gear ratio is wrong: it's slipping or not in the gear it should be. Continuing to drive can make internal damage worse.
c: Low or burnt transmission fluid (check first)
Faulty shift solenoid or valve body
k: Check fluid level and condition using the manufacturer's procedure (dark or burnt-smelling fluid is a bad sign)
Drive gently until it's diagnosed

blocks.m: The torque converter clutch isn't engaging (or its circuit is faulty). This raises fluid temperature and hurts fuel economy.
k: Check fluid level and condition
At steady highway speed with lockup, RPM should drop slightly

blocks.m: Shift solenoid fault. The transmission may be stuck in one gear or shift poorly.
k: Check fluid level and condition
Inspect the transmission connector for fluid wicking into it

blocks.m: Braking/stability systems – ABS or traction control may be disabled.
Transmission fluid pressure is low. Low pressure makes clutches slip and can damage the transmission quickly.
k: Check the fluid level immediately
Avoid hard acceleration until it's diagnosed

blocks.m: Generic powertrain code (hybrid propulsion).
Diesel/advanced emissions after-treatment – may lead to reduced power if ignored.
Fuel trim based on the downstream O2 sensor is at its limit.
k: Look for exhaust leaks
Check whether P0420/P0430 or fuel trim codes are also present

blocks.m: The two accelerator pedal position sensors disagree. The car usually goes into reduced-power mode.
c: Worn accelerator pedal sensor (replaced as a pedal assembly)
Wiring or connector fault at the pedal
k: Pedal D and E readings should rise together smoothly as you press the pedal

blocks.m: The upstream O2 sensor signal is stuck lean or rich.
c: A real lean condition (vacuum leak, exhaust leak) or rich condition (leaking injector)
k: Check fuel trims and look for vacuum/exhaust leaks before replacing the sensor

blocks.m: The downstream O2 sensor signal is stuck lean or rich.
k: Look for exhaust leaks around the converter and sensor

blocks.m: Cylinder deactivation system – may cause rough running or reduced economy.
Problem on the high-speed CAN network that the modules use to talk to each other. Many systems may act strangely at once.
c: Damaged or corroded wiring or connectors (water intrusion, accident damage)
A failed module disrupting the network
Poorly installed aftermarket accessories (remote start, alarms)
k: Check battery voltage first
Think about any recent repairs, accessory installs or water leaks
Note which modules report U-codes; the one they all lost contact with is the suspect

blocks.m: Module communication – often low battery voltage, connectors or a module offline.
Network code – often low battery voltage, connectors or a module offline.
A module lost communication with the engine or transmission computer.
c: A brief low-voltage event (weak battery, jump start, battery change)
Loose or corroded connector at the engine/transmission computer
k: If the car drives normally, test the battery, clear codes and see if it returns
Check the connectors and grounds at the module

blocks.m: Lost communication with the ABS module. ABS and stability control are likely disabled.
k: Check whether the ABS/traction warning lights are on
Drive carefully on slippery roads until fixed

blocks.m: Communication problem with a safety-related module – ABS, stability, airbag or steering functions may be disabled.
Lost communication with the body control module or instrument cluster. Lights, locks or gauges may misbehave.
k: Check battery voltage
Note which features stopped working

blocks.m: Lost communication with the airbag (restraints) module. The airbags may not deploy in a crash.
c: Connector or wiring fault (often under a seat)
k: Check whether the airbag warning light is on
Have it repaired promptly: this is a safety system

blocks.m: Hybrid/electric drive system – have it checked promptly.
